method.population: Every figure on this page is computed each night from the live charter offers of the {priced, number} boats based {where} that have at least one bookable 7-night charter in the next 12 months. The month tables cover charters starting from {from} to {to}.
method.median: The typical week is the median weekly price: half of the priced charter weeks cost less, half cost more. The middle half is the range between the 25th and the 75th percentile of those weeks, so the cheapest and the most expensive quarter are left out.
method.panel: Within each table the months compare like with like: they are priced over the same boats, those with a price in at least three of every four months shown. A month appears only when at least half as many boats have a price in it as in the best-covered month, so thin off-season months are left out. Weeks priced under 300 € are placeholders and never count, and figures based on fewer than 5 boats are not shown.
method.costs: Prices are for the boat per charter week, as published by our partners. A skipper, obligatory extras and the security deposit come on top. Skipper and deposit figures are medians over the boats that list them. Obligatory extras are the per-boat fees for a week; a boat without any counts as having none. Per-person items such as tourist tax are not included, and boats with a percentage-based fee (APA on crewed yachts) are left out.

hub.lede: What a yacht charter week really costs, computed every night from the live prices of {boats, number} boats. Each guide shows the typical weekly price month by month and by boat type, with skipper, extras and deposit.
hub.note: Typical week: the lowest and the highest monthly median over the next 12 months, for the boat per week. Updated {date}. Amounts in euros (EUR).
hub.read1: Every figure on this page is the price of the boat for one week, as the partner fleets publish it for the coming twelve months: the same total a booking shows before extras. It is not a per-night rate and not a price per person. The typical week is the median of all priced weeks that start in a month, so a few very cheap or very expensive boats do not move it; the range in the table runs from the cheapest to the most expensive month of the year.
hub.read2: On top of the weekly price you should plan for the obligatory extras collected at the base (final cleaning, bed linen, transit log, tourist tax), a skipper if you do not hold a licence, fuel and mooring fees on the way, and a refundable security deposit that is blocked on a card at check-in. The country guides list the typical amounts for each of these, so the weekly price and the real total can be read side by side.

hub.saveHeading: When a charter week costs less
hub.save1: The season sets the price. July and August are the most expensive weeks almost everywhere in the Mediterranean; the same boat costs noticeably less in May, June, September and early October, when the weather is still reliable and the marinas are quieter. Where a country's season runs differently, the guide's month table shows it.
hub.save2: Booking early keeps the choice; booking late can lower the price. Popular models and the best weeks are gone months ahead, and early-booking discounts reward those who decide in autumn or winter. Weeks that are still free a few weeks before departure often come with genuine last-minute cuts — worth a look when the dates are flexible.
hub.save3: The boat itself matters as much as the month. A catamaran costs more than a monohull of the same length but sleeps more people, so the price per cabin can be similar; a five-year-old boat is cheaper than a new one of the same model; and a motor yacht adds fuel to the weekly price. Comparing the price per cabin between boat types is usually the fairest way to decide.
